claim: The structure of the Escherichia coli 70S ribosome was determined using cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) with a global resolution of 2.0 Å.
source: Using cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM), we determined the structure of the Escherichia coli 70S ribosome with a global resolution of 2.0 Å.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the method used (cryo-EM) and the resolution achieved (2.0 Å), which is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The cryo-EM maps reveal unambiguous positioning of protein and RNA residues.
source: The maps reveal unambiguous positioning of protein and RNA residues, their detailed chemical interactions, and chemical modifications.
evidence: This claim is supported by the high-resolution maps and detailed structural models presented throughout the manuscript, including figures showing clear density for individual residues.

claim: The maps reveal the first examples of isopeptide and thioamide backbone substitutions in ribosomal proteins.
source: Notable features include the first examples of isopeptide and thioamide backbone substitutions in ribosomal proteins, the former likely conserved in all domains of life.
evidence: The manuscript presents cryo-EM density and structural models showing these modifications, along with supporting mass spectrometry data for the thioamide.

claim: The isopeptide modification in ribosomal proteins is likely conserved in all domains of life.
source: Notable features include the first examples of isopeptide and thioamide backbone substitutions in ribosomal proteins, the former likely conserved in all domains of life.
evidence: This claim is supported by phylogenetic analysis showing conservation of the sequence motif containing the isoaspartate across bacteria, archaea, and eukaryotes, and by remodeling of archaeal and eukaryotic structures.

claim: The maps reveal extensive solvation of the small (30S) ribosomal subunit.
source: The maps also reveal extensive solvation of the small (30S) ribosomal subunit, and interactions with A-site and P-site tRNAs, mRNA, and the antibiotic paromomycin.
evidence: The manuscript presents models with thousands of water molecules and detailed figures showing solvation patterns.

claim: The maps reveal interactions with A-site and P-site tRNAs, mRNA, and the antibiotic paromomycin.
source: The maps also reveal extensive solvation of the small (30S) ribosomal subunit, and interactions with A-site and P-site tRNAs, mRNA, and the antibiotic paromomycin.
evidence: Detailed structural models and figures showing these interactions are presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The ribosome varies in size from 2.3 MDa to over 4 MDa across the three domains of life.
source: The ribosome performs the crucial task of translating the genetic code into proteins and varies in size from 2.3 MDa to over 4 MDa across the three domains of life (Melnikov et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Polypeptide synthesis occurs in the peptidyl transferase center (PTC).
source: Polypeptide synthesis occurs in the peptidyl transferase center (PTC), where the ribosome acts primarily as an 'entropic trap' for peptide bond formation (Rodnina, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by a citation.

claim: The ribosome acts primarily as an 'entropic trap' for peptide bond formation.
source: Polypeptide synthesis occurs in the peptidyl transferase center (PTC), where the ribosome acts primarily as an 'entropic trap' for peptide bond formation (Rodnina, 2013).
evidence: This mechanistic interpretation is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The ribosome is naturally the target of a plurality of antibiotics with diverse mechanisms of action.
source: Because of the ribosome's essential role in supporting life, it is naturally the target of a plurality of antibiotics with diverse mechanisms of action (Arenz and Wilson, 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The resolution of available X-ray crystal structures of the ribosome in key functional states remains too low to provide accurate models of non-covalent bonding.
source: Although X-ray crystallography has been central in revealing the molecular basis of many steps in translation, the resolution of available X-ray crystal structures of the ribosome in key functional states remains too low to provide accurate models of non-covalent bonding, that is, hydrogen bonding, van der Waals contacts, and ionic interactions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the typical resolution limits of X-ray crystallography for ribosome structures.

claim: The development of small-molecule drugs such as antibiotics is hampered at the typical resolution of available X-ray crystal structures of the ribosome (~3 Å).
source: Furthermore, the development of small-molecule drugs such as antibiotics is hampered at the typical resolution of available X-ray crystal structures of the ribosome (~3 Å) (Arenz and Wilson, 2016; Yusupova and Yusupov, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature discussing limitations of current structural data for drug development.

claim: Previous high-resolution structures of the bacterial ribosome include X-ray crystal structures of the Escherichia coli ribosome at 2.4 Å (2.1 Å by CC ½).
source: Previous high-resolution structures of the bacterial ribosome include X-ray crystal structures of the Escherichia coli ribosome at 2.4 Å (2.1 Å by CC ½; Noeske et al., 2015) and Thermus thermophilus ribosome at 2.3 Å (Polikanov et al., 2015), and cryo-EM reconstructions at 2.1–2.3 Å (Halfon et al., 2019; Pichkur et al., 2020; Stojković et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a factual statement about prior work, supported by citations.

claim: Previous high-resolution structures of the bacterial ribosome include X-ray crystal structures of the Thermus thermophilus ribosome at 2.3 Å.
source: Previous high-resolution structures of the bacterial ribosome include X-ray crystal structures of the Escherichia coli ribosome at 2.4 Å (2.1 Å by CC ½; Noeske et al., 2015) and Thermus thermophilus ribosome at 2.3 Å (Polikanov et al., 2015), and cryo-EM reconstructions at 2.1–2.3 Å (Halfon et al., 2019; Pichkur et al., 2020; Stojković et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a factual statement about prior work, supported by citations.

claim: Previous high-resolution structures of the bacterial ribosome include cryo-EM reconstructions at 2.1–2.3 Å.
source: Previous high-resolution structures of the bacterial ribosome include X-ray crystal structures of the Escherichia coli ribosome at 2.4 Å (2.1 Å by CC ½; Noeske et al., 2015) and Thermus thermophilus ribosome at 2.3 Å (Polikanov et al., 2015), and cryo-EM reconstructions at 2.1–2.3 Å (Halfon et al., 2019; Pichkur et al., 2020; Stojković et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a factual statement about prior work, supported by citations.

claim: The 'gold-standard' FSC is more precisely a measure of self-consistency of the data.
source: However, the 'gold-standard' FSC (GS-FSC) most commonly reported, wherein random halves of the particles are refined independently and correlation of the two half-maps is calculated as a function of spatial frequency, is more precisely a measure of self-consistency of the data (Henderson et al., 2012; Rosenthal and Henderson, 2003; Subramaniam et al., 2016).
evidence: This interpretation of the GS-FSC metric is supported by citations to methodological literature.

claim: The map-to-model FSC compares the cryo-EM experimental map to the structural model derived from it.
source: A separate measure, the map-to-model FSC, compares the cryo-EM experimental map to the structural model derived from it (DiMaio et al., 2013; Liebschner et al., 2019; Subramaniam et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a definition of a methodological metric, supported by citations.

claim: The structure of the E. coli 70S ribosome was determined to a global resolution of 2.0 Å, with higher resolution up to 1.8 Å in the best-resolved core regions of the 50S subunit.
source: Here we determined the structure of the E. coli 70S ribosome to a global resolution of 2.0 Å, with higher resolution up to 1.8 Å in the best-resolved core regions of the 50S subunit.
evidence: This is supported by the resolution analysis and local resolution maps presented in the manuscript.

claim: The final maps were generated from two 70S ribosome complexes that were formed separately using P-site tRNAfMet that differed only by being charged with two different non-amino acid monomers.
source: Our final maps were generated from two 70S ribosome complexes that were formed separately using P-site tRNAfMet that differed only by being charged with two different non-amino acid monomers (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the experimental design, which is detailed in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Both complexes yielded structures in the same functional state, with similar occupancy of the tRNAs.
source: In both complexes, we used the same mRNA and A-site Val-tRNAVal. Both complexes yielded structures in the same functional state, with similar occupancy of the tRNAs.
evidence: This is an observation from the structural analysis of the two datasets.

claim: Neither A-site nor P-site tRNA 3'-CCA-ends were resolved in the individual cryo-EM maps.
source: As neither A-site nor P-site tRNA 3'-CCA-ends were resolved in the individual cryo-EM maps, we merged the two datasets for the final reconstructions (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM data analysis.

claim: After Ewald sphere correction in RELION, global resolution of the entire complex reached 1.98 Å resolution by GS-FSC.
source: After Ewald sphere correction in RELION (Zivanov et al., 2018), global resolution of the entire complex reached 1.98 Å resolution by GS-FSC, with local resolution reaching 1.8 Å (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by the FSC curves and resolution maps presented in the figures and tables.

claim: The local resolution reached 1.8 Å.
source: After Ewald sphere correction in RELION (Zivanov et al., 2018), global resolution of the entire complex reached 1.98 Å resolution by GS-FSC, with local resolution reaching 1.8 Å (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by the local resolution maps shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The global resolution reached 2.04 Å using the map-to-model FSC criterion.
source: The global resolution reached 2.04 Å using the map-to-model FSC criterion (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the map-to-model FSC curve shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Focused refinement of the 30S subunit improved its map quality substantially, along with its immediate contacts to the 50S subunit and the mRNA and tRNA anticodon stem-loops.
source: In particular, focused refinement of the 30S subunit improved its map quality substantially, along with its immediate contacts to the 50S subunit and the mRNA and tRNA anticodon stem-loops.
evidence: This is an observation from the focused refinement analysis, supported by the improved resolution and map quality.

claim: The high resolution indicated by the FSC curves is supported by several visual features observable in the maps, including holes in many aromatic rings and riboses.
source: The high resolution indicated by the FSC curves is supported by several visual features observable in the maps, including holes in many aromatic rings and riboses, as well as ring puckers, the directionality of non-bridging phosphate oxygens in ribosomal RNA, and numerous well-resolved ions, water molecules, and small molecules (Figure 1B–D, Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: These features are shown in the figures and are characteristic of high-resolution structures.

claim: The maps reveal known post-transcriptional and post-translational modifications of ribosomal RNA and proteins in detail.
source: The maps also reveal known post-transcriptional and post-translational modifications of ribosomal RNA and proteins in detail (Figure 1—figure supplement 5, Figure 1—figure supplement 6), many of which are as previously described (Fischer et al., 2015; Noeske et al., 2015; Polikanov et al., 2015; Stojković et al., 2020).
evidence: The modifications are shown in the figures and are consistent with prior literature.

claim: Elements of the ribosome at the periphery are less ordered, including the uL1 arm, the GTPase activating center, bL12 proteins, and the central portion of the A-site finger in the 50S subunit.
source: As seen in other ribosome structures, elements of the ribosome at the periphery are less ordered, including the uL1 arm, the GTPase activating center, bL12 proteins, and the central portion of the A-site finger in the 50S subunit (23S rRNA helix H38), as well as the periphery of the 30S subunit head domain and spur (16S rRNA helix h6).
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM maps, consistent with prior structures.

claim: The resolution of the maps for the elbow and acceptor ends of the P-site and A-site tRNAs is relatively low, likely as a result of poor accommodation of the unnatural substrates used.
source: The resolution of the maps for the elbow and acceptor ends of the P-site and A-site tRNAs is also relatively low, likely as a result of poor accommodation of the unnatural substrates used.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observed map quality and the experimental design.

claim: The 30S ribosomal subunit is highly dynamic in carrying out its role in the translation cycle.
source: The 30S ribosomal subunit is highly dynamic in carrying out its role in the translation cycle (Munro et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The 30S subunit exhibits more flexibility than the core of the 50S subunit even in defined conformational states of the ribosome.
source: Previously published structures demonstrate that even in defined conformational states of the ribosome, the 30S subunit exhibits more flexibility than the core of the 50S subunit.
evidence: This is an inference based on prior structural studies.

claim: The mass of the 50S subunit dominates alignments in cryo-EM reconstructions of the 70S ribosome.
source: Furthermore, the mass of the 50S subunit dominates alignments in cryo-EM reconstructions of the 70S ribosome.
evidence: This is a known technical consideration in cryo-EM of the ribosome.

claim: Solvation of the 30S subunit has not been extensively modeled in prior structures.
source: Solvation of the 30S subunit has not been extensively modeled, again owing to the fact that it is generally more flexible and less well-resolved than the 50S subunit, even in available high-resolution structures (Noeske et al., 2015; Polikanov et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an observation about prior work, supported by citations.

claim: The tight binding of tRNA to the P site is reflected in extensive direct contacts between the tRNA anticodon stem-loop (ASL) and both the 30S subunit head and platform domains.
source: The tight binding of tRNA to the P site (Lill et al., 1986) is reflected in extensive direct contacts between the tRNA anticodon stem-loop (ASL) and both the 30S subunit head and platform domains (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data shown in Figure 2 and by prior biochemical studies.

claim: The C-terminal residues Lys129 and Arg130 of protein uS9 form ionic and hydrogen bonding interactions with the nucleotides in the U-turn motif of the P-site ASL.
source: The C-terminal residues Lys129 and Arg130 of protein uS9, which are important for translational fidelity (Arora et al., 2013), form ionic and hydrogen bonding interactions with the nucleotides in the U-turn motif of the P-site ASL, and Arg130 stacks with the base of U33 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by the structural model shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Arg130 of protein uS9 stacks with the base of U33 in the P-site tRNA.
source: The C-terminal residues Lys129 and Arg130 of protein uS9, which are important for translational fidelity (Arora et al., 2013), form ionic and hydrogen bonding interactions with the nucleotides in the U-turn motif of the P-site ASL, and Arg130 stacks with the base of U33 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by the structural model shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The C-terminal tails of ribosomal proteins uS13 and uS19 are not visible in the map, suggesting they do not make specific contacts with the tRNA when the ribosome is in the unrotated state.
source: However, the C-terminal tails of ribosomal proteins uS13 and uS19, which come from the 30S subunit head domain and are lysine-rich, are not visible in the map, suggesting they do not make specific contacts with the tRNA when the ribosome is in the unrotated state.
evidence: This is an inference based on the absence of density in the cryo-EM map.

claim: Direct interactions between A-site tRNA and the 30S subunit are highly localized to the top of helices h44 and h18 in 16S rRNA and to helix H69 in 23S rRNA.
source: Direct interactions between A-site tRNA and the 30S subunit are highly localized to the top of helices h44 and h18 in 16S rRNA and to helix H69 in 23S rRNA (i.e. 16S rRNA nucleotides G530, A1492, and A1493, and 23S rRNA nucleotide A1913).
evidence: This is supported by the structural model and is consistent with known interactions in the decoding center.

claim: Contacts between the A-site tRNA and 30S subunit head domain are entirely solvent mediated apart from nucleotide C1054.
source: By contrast, contacts between the A-site tRNA and 30S subunit head domain are entirely solvent mediated (Figure 2E) apart from nucleotide C1054, possibly reflecting the weaker binding of tRNA to the A site (Lill et al., 1986) and the need for A-site tRNA conformational dynamics during mRNA decoding (Rodnina et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the structural model shown in Figure 2E and by prior biochemical and biophysical studies.

claim: Protein bS21 resides near the path of mRNA on the 30S subunit platform.
source: Protein bS21, which resides near the path of mRNA on the 30S subunit platform (Held et al., 1973; Marzi et al., 2007; Sashital et al., 2014), is essential in E. coli (Bubunenko et al., 2007; Goodall et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Protein bS21 is essential in E. coli.
source: Protein bS21, which resides near the path of mRNA on the 30S subunit platform (Held et al., 1973; Marzi et al., 2007; Sashital et al., 2014), is essential in E. coli (Bubunenko et al., 2007; Goodall et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Structural disorder in the bS21 region has precluded modeling of the C-terminus in prior structures.
source: Although partial structural models of bS21 have been determined (Fischer et al., 2015; Noeske et al., 2015), structural disorder in this region has precluded modeling of the C-terminus.
evidence: This is an observation about prior work, supported by citations.

claim: In the present maps, low-pass filtering provides clear evidence for the conformation of the entire bS21 protein chain, including 13 amino acids at the C-terminus that extend to the base of the 30S subunit head domain.
source: In the present maps, low-pass filtering provides clear evidence for the conformation of the entire protein chain, including 13 amino acids at the C-terminus that extend to the base of the 30S subunit head domain (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM density shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Most of the C-terminal residues of bS21 are found in an alpha-helical conformation near the Shine-Dalgarno helix.
source: Most of the C-terminal residues are found in an alpha-helical conformation near the Shine-Dalgarno helix formed between the 3' end of 16S rRNA and the mRNA ribosome binding site (Shine and Dalgarno, 1975), while the C-terminal arginine-leucine-tyrosine (RLY) motif makes close contacts with 16S rRNA helix h37 and nucleotide A1167 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by the structural model shown in Figure 3.

claim: The C-terminal arginine-leucine-tyrosine (RLY) motif of bS21 makes close contacts with 16S rRNA helix h37 and nucleotide A1167.
source: Most of the C-terminal residues are found in an alpha-helical conformation near the Shine-Dalgarno helix formed between the 3' end of 16S rRNA and the mRNA ribosome binding site (Shine and Dalgarno, 1975), while the C-terminal arginine-leucine-tyrosine (RLY) motif makes close contacts with 16S rRNA helix h37 and nucleotide A1167 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by the structural model shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The arginine and leucine residues of the RLY motif pack in the minor groove of helix h37.
source: The arginine and leucine residues pack in the minor groove of helix h37, and the terminal tyrosine stacks on A1167.
evidence: This is supported by the structural model shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The terminal tyrosine of the RLY motif stacks on A1167.
source: The arginine and leucine residues pack in the minor groove of helix h37, and the terminal tyrosine stacks on A1167.
evidence: This is supported by the structural model shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Multiple sequence alignment of bS21 sequences from distinct bacterial phyla revealed that the RLY C-terminal motif is conserved in bS21 sequences of the Gammaproteobacteria phylum.
source: Multiple sequence alignment of bS21 sequences from distinct bacterial phyla revealed that the RLY C-terminal motif is conserved in bS21 sequences of the Gammaproteobacteria phylum while in Betaproteobacteria, the sibling group of Gammaproteobacteria, bS21 sequences possess a lysine-leucine-tyrosine (KLY) C-terminal motif instead (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by the sequence alignment shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In Betaproteobacteria, bS21 sequences possess a lysine-leucine-tyrosine (KLY) C-terminal motif instead of RLY.
source: Multiple sequence alignment of bS21 sequences from distinct bacterial phyla revealed that the RLY C-terminal motif is conserved in bS21 sequences of the Gammaproteobacteria phylum while in Betaproteobacteria, the sibling group of Gammaproteobacteria, bS21 sequences possess a lysine-leucine-tyrosine (KLY) C-terminal motif instead (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by the sequence alignment shown in Figure 3C.

claim: C-terminal extensions (RLY or KLY) are absent in bS21 from other bacterial phyla.
source: Interestingly, such C-terminal extensions (RLY or KLY) are absent in other bacterial phyla (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the sequence alignments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Putative homologs of bS21 were identified in huge bacteriophages.
source: Recently, putative homologs of bS21 were identified in huge bacteriophages, which were shown to harbor genes encoding components of the translational machinery (Al-Shayeb et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a factual statement about prior work, supported by a citation.

claim: Some phage S21 homologs contain KLY-like motifs.
source: Inspection of sequence alignments reveals that some phage S21 homologs also contain KLY-like motifs (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by the sequence alignment shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The presence of phage S21 homologs containing KLY-like motifs is consistent with the host range of these phages.
source: The presence of phage S21 homologs containing KLY-like motifs is consistent with the host range of these phages (Figure 3C, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the phylogenetic analysis and sequence data.

claim: Ribosomal protein uS11 is a central component of the 30S subunit platform domain.
source: Ribosomal protein uS11 is a central component of the 30S subunit platform domain and assembles cooperatively with ribosomal proteins uS6 and uS18 (Stern et al., 1988), preceding the binding of bS21 late in 30S subunit maturation (Held et al., 1973; Sashital et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Protein uS11 assembles cooperatively with ribosomal proteins uS6 and uS18.
source: Ribosomal protein uS11 is a central component of the 30S subunit platform domain and assembles cooperatively with ribosomal proteins uS6 and uS18 (Stern et al., 1988), preceding the binding of bS21 late in 30S subunit maturation (Held et al., 1973; Sashital et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Protein uS11 makes intimate contact with 16S rRNA residues in a 3-helix junction that forms part of the 30S subunit E site.
source: Protein uS11 makes intimate contact with 16S rRNA residues in a 3-helix junction that forms part of the 30S subunit E site and stabilizes the 16S rRNA that forms the platform component of the P site (Stern et al., 1988).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: An inspection of the 30S subunit map uncovered a previously unmodeled isoaspartyl residue in protein uS11, at the encoded residue N119.
source: Remarkably, an inspection of the 30S subunit map uncovered a previously unmodeled isoaspartyl residue in protein uS11, at the encoded residue N119 (Figure 4; see Materials and methods), marking the first identified protein backbone modification in the ribosome.
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM density shown in Figure 4 and by the modeling described in Materials and methods.

claim: The isoaspartyl residue at position 119 in uS11 marks the first identified protein backbone modification in the ribosome.
source: Remarkably, an inspection of the 30S subunit map uncovered a previously unmodeled isoaspartyl residue in protein uS11, at the encoded residue N119 (Figure 4; see Materials and methods), marking the first identified protein backbone modification in the ribosome.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the finding, based on the structural data.

claim: It has been known that the isoaspartate modification can exist in uS11.
source: While it has been known that this modification can exist in uS11 (David et al., 1999), its functional significance has remained unclear, and prior structures did not have the resolution to pinpoint its exact location.
evidence: This is a factual statement about prior work, supported by a citation.

claim: Prior structures did not have the resolution to pinpoint the exact location of the isoaspartate in uS11.
source: While it has been known that this modification can exist in uS11 (David et al., 1999), its functional significance has remained unclear, and prior structures did not have the resolution to pinpoint its exact location.
evidence: This is an observation about prior work.

claim: Conversion of asparagine to isoaspartate inserts an additional methylene group into the backbone (the Cβ position) and generates a methylcarboxylate side chain.
source: Conversion of asparagine to isoaspartate inserts an additional methylene group into the backbone (the Cβ position) and generates a methylcarboxylate side chain (Reissner and Aswad, 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the chemistry of isoaspartate formation, supported by a citation.

claim: In the present map, the shapes of the backbone density and proximal residues in the chain reveal the presence of the additional methylene in the isoaspartate.
source: In the present map, the shapes of the backbone density and proximal residues in the chain reveal the presence of the additional methylene, allowing it the flexibility to pack closely with the contacting rRNA nucleotides (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM density shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: A 30S-focused reconstruction using only early movie frames shows improved density for the isoaspartate sidechain, albeit at slightly lower resolution overall.
source: A 30S-focused reconstruction using only early movie frames, in which damage to carboxylates would not be as severe (Marques et al., 2019), shows improved density for the IAS sidechain, albeit at slightly lower resolution overall (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM density shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and by the rationale that early frames have less radiation damage.

claim: Investigation of residues flanking the isoaspartate in uS11 reveals near-universal conservation in bacteria, chloroplasts, and mitochondria.
source: Investigation of residues flanking the isoaspartate in uS11 reveals near-universal conservation in bacteria, chloroplasts, and mitochondria (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 2), suggesting that the isoaspartate may contribute to 30S subunit assembly or stability.
evidence: This is supported by the sequence logos and phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The isoaspartate in uS11 may contribute to 30S subunit assembly or stability.
source: Investigation of residues flanking the isoaspartate in uS11 reveals near-universal conservation in bacteria, chloroplasts, and mitochondria (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 2), suggesting that the isoaspartate may contribute to 30S subunit assembly or stability.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the conservation pattern and structural context.

claim: The isoaspartate allows high shape complementarity including van der Waals contacts and hydrogen bonds between this region of uS11 and the 16S rRNA it contacts.
source: Consistent with this idea, the isoaspartate allows high shape complementarity including van der Waals contacts and hydrogen bonds between this region of uS11 and the 16S rRNA it contacts, which involves three consecutive purine-purine base pairs in bacteria (Supplementary file 2), and a change in rRNA helical direction that is capped by stacking of histidine 118 in uS11 on a conserved purine (A718 in E. coli; Figure 4B, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by the structural model shown in Figure 4B and the sequence analysis in Supplementary file 2.

claim: The sequence motif in bacterial uS11 containing the isoaspartate is also conserved in a domain-specific manner in archaea and eukaryotes.
source: Strikingly, the sequence motif in bacterial uS11 is also conserved in a domain-specific manner in archaea and eukaryotes (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), as are the rRNA residues near the predicted isoAsp (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by the sequence logos shown in Figure 4C and the phylogenetic analysis in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The rRNA residues near the predicted isoaspartate are conserved in archaea and eukaryotes.
source: Strikingly, the sequence motif in bacterial uS11 is also conserved in a domain-specific manner in archaea and eukaryotes (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), as are the rRNA residues near the predicted isoAsp (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by the sequence analysis in Supplementary file 2.

claim: Remodeling the isoaspartate motifs in maps from recently-published cryo-EM reconstructions of an archaeal 30S ribosomal subunit complex and a yeast 80S ribosome complex shows that the isoaspartate also seems to be present in these organisms based on the residue-level correlation between map and model.
source: Remodeling the isoAsp motifs in maps from recently-published cryo-EM reconstructions of an archaeal 30S ribosomal subunit complex at 2.8 Å resolution (Nürenberg-Goloub et al., 2020) and a yeast 80S ribosome complex at 2.6 Å resolution (Tesina et al., 2020) shows that the isoaspartate also seems to be present in these organisms based on the residue-level correlation between map and model (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the remodeling analysis and correlation plots shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The phylogenetic data and structural data indicate that the isoaspartate in uS11 is nearly universally conserved.
source: Taken together, the phylogenetic data and structural data indicate that the isoaspartate in uS11 is nearly universally conserved, highlighting its likely important role in ribosome assembly and function.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined phylogenetic and structural evidence.

claim: The E. coli 30S ribosomal subunit has eleven post-transcriptionally modified nucleotides in 16S rRNA.
source: The E. coli 30S ribosomal subunit has eleven post-transcriptionally modified nucleotides in 16S rRNA, all of which can be seen in the present maps or inferred from hydrogen bonding patterns in the cases of many pseudouridines.
evidence: This is supported by the structural data and is consistent with known modifications.

claim: Two methylated nucleotides–m7G527 and m62A1519–appear not to be fully modified, based on the density at ~2.1 Å resolution.
source: Interestingly, two methylated nucleotides–m7G527 and m62A1519–appear not to be fully modified, based on the density at ~2.1 Å resolution (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM density shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: In the map, m7G527 appears partially methylated.
source: In the map, m7G527 appears partially methylated, and m62A1519 lacks one of the two methyl groups.
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM density.

claim: m62A1519 lacks one of the two methyl groups.
source: In the map, m7G527 appears partially methylated, and m62A1519 lacks one of the two methyl groups.
evidence: This is an observation from the cryo-EM density.

claim: Loss of methylation at m7G527 has been shown to confer low-level streptomycin resistance.
source: Loss of methylation at m7G527, which is located near the mRNA decoding site, has been shown to confer low-level streptomycin resistance (Okamoto et al., 2007), and possibly neomycin resistance in some cases (Mikheil et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Loss of methylation at m7G527 possibly confers neomycin resistance in some cases.
source: Loss of methylation at m7G527, which is located near the mRNA decoding site, has been shown to confer low-level streptomycin resistance (Okamoto et al., 2007), and possibly neomycin resistance in some cases (Mikheil et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

source: With regard to resolution, in this work, we have supplemented the reporting of the 'gold-standard' FSC with map-to-model FSC curves for our maps and for comparisons to previous work. source: For example, maps from recent cryo-EM reconstructions of the bacterial 50S ribosomal subunit report resolutions of ~2.1 Å–2.3 Å but the deposited models reach global resolutions of ~2.3 Å–2.5 Å by the map-to-model FSC criterion (Halfon et al., 2019; Pichkur et al., 2020; Stojković et al., 2020; see Materials and methods; Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the map-to-model FSC calculations shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

source: Notably, for the 2.1 Å map of the E. coli 50S subunit based on half-map FSC values (Pichkur et al., 2020), the map-to-model FSC fit of our 50S subunit model to that map has a higher resolution (2.07 Å), compared to the deposited model (2.29 Å, PDB entry 6xz7; Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the map-to-model FSC calculations shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

evidence: This is an explanation of the rationale for using the map-to-model FSC.

claim: Methods for refining heterogeneous maps have proliferated, but ways to work with and create a model from many maps of the same complex have not yet been standardized and require substantial manual intervention.
source: Aside from global high resolution, the conformational heterogeneity of the ribosome also calls attention to the tools used for working with complexes that display variable resolution. Methods for refining heterogeneous maps have proliferated, including multi-body refinement (Nakane et al., 2018) and 3D variability analysis (Punjani and Fleet, 2020) among others, but ways to work with and create a model from many maps of the same complex have not yet been standardized and require substantial manual intervention.
evidence: This is an observation about the current state of methods in the field.
